messages.subject: Best methods for saving graphics?
messages.body_plain:
Hello D-RUGies,

I am looking for some advice regarding the creation of publication-quality graphs in R. My graphs are simple bar charts, created using ggplot2 in R studio. I have tried writing files to various graphics devices (pdf, tiff, jpeg, etc), but the files look crappy when I open them in MS Word, even if I increase the ppi. Bitmaps look blurry and pdfs delete lines seemingly at random. Same if I save directly from the graphics window in R Studio (where they look so nice!). Copying and pasting metafiles seems to look best in Word, but I don't think publications will accept this format.

Has anyone else encountered this problem and figured out a solution?

Many thanks,
Emily

Emily Peffer
PhD candidate
Graduate Group in Ecology
Department of Plant Sciences
University of California, Davis
Office: (530) 752-2667

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Best methods for saving graphics?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

.pdf and .eps files are usually fine for publications because they are vector based graphics. If you make a .pdf try it with the option bg = "white" to set the background color, that may fix your disappearing lines.

To make an eps (encapsulated post script) or a high res image  you can play around with the following commands and tweak them as you see fit:

postscript(file="Model.eps",width=6.8,height=4.5)

or

tiff(file="Model.tiff",width=6.8,height=4.5,units="in",type="quartz",res=600)

--

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Best methods for saving graphics?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

I'm planning on giving a talk on making graphics for publication in R in a few weeks! But I havn't had the problems with pdfs deleting lines that you have had. What function do you use to export the figure? If you are using the "export plot" button, you may not be able to get the specifics you need, so I always use the "pdf" fucntion. There are equivalent functions for any other graphics formats. But as Jamie said, publications tend to specify file type and ask that figures be uploaded separately. You can also export it as an svg file and manipulate the image in Inkscape or other graphics software. (inkscape is free!)

pdf(file = "sleepplot.pdf", width= 6, height = 4, # specify width and hight in inches
    useDingbats=F) # I have had trouble when uploading figures with digbats before, so I don't use them

sleepplot2 # print our plot

dev.off() # stop making pdfs

Rosie,

I have used the code you suggested. I should say that lines are not actually being deleted, but certain lines disappear when I insert the pdf into Word. When I re-size the figures, different lines disappear! Like magic!

I guess I have two issues: (1) Creating nice-looking graphs in file formats that are accepted by the journal (what I'm reading online has conflicting info for what formats are accepted for this particular journal, but they seem to want bitmaps), and (2) having some graphics that look decent enough in the Word doc so I can send the doc out for review without additional attachments and have them embedded for when I submit my dissertation.

I will play around with the suggestions given thus far. Thanks all!

Emily

messages.subject: Re: Best methods for saving graphics?
messages.body_plain:
Just to chime in and add one quick option, "ggsave".  If you are plotting a ggplot object, you can use ggsave for most of the file types that have been mentioned. Each journal generally will have specifics for size, dpi and type and it's probably best to use the specific call for each.  However, for word docs, I think ggsave as .png's has worked well for all sorts of graphics. I've had a few little bugs here and there, but generally they are solved by using dev.off() and then rexporting.  Give it a shot.  Hope this helps.

Example:

ggsave("figure_1A.png", width=8, height=6, dpi=300)

# Or

ggsave("figure_1B.pdf", width=8, height=6)

Ryan Peek
Center for Watershed Sciences
Aquatic Ecologist

messages.subject_clean: Mixed model presentation, R users group, Wednesday, 1-3 pm Wickson 2124
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Tomorrow - at 1 pm in Wickson 2124 - Lindsay Henderson will be presenting on some heirarchical mixed model results she is looking for feedback on:

Description:

> My experiment used a repeated measure design to investigate predatory fishes' behaviour under three chemosensory treatments. I wanted to assess whether fish spent different amounts of time in different parts of their tank (defined as 3 zones), or whether they behaved differently within each zone dependent upon the chemosensory treatment experienced. To analyse these data I used hierarchical mixed models, and I found a significant interaction between chemosensory treatment and zone. I would like to understand how to use post-hoc tests to interpret this result.

Hope to see you there,
Stella

messages.subject: Tomorrow: Modeling geographic variation in tree allometry
messages.subject_clean: Tomorrow: Modeling geographic variation in tree allometry
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Tomorrow Catherine Hulshof will present a case study for feedback at the D-RUG meeting.  From Catherine:

> Using the Forest Inventory and Analysis National Program database, I investigated the geographic distribution and underlying determinants of tree height-diameter allometries. I quantified the effects of forest stand density and climate on height-diameter relationships for 300 tree species across the United States by using spatial simultaneous auto-regression models in combination with a null model-based test of assembly. I also extracted the residuals from species specific height-diameter relationships to understand the effects of climate and forest structure on within-species variability in growth strategies. I would like to brainstorm additional analyses that may be used to determine the influence of climate and forest structure on intraspecific variation in height-diameter allometries.

We'll have our regular Q&A and work session in the second half.  See you at the regular place and time: 2124 Wickson, 1-3PM.

Noam

messages.subject: NLS headaches
messages.body_plain:
Howdy,

I've been banging my head against the wall about this for awhile now and perhaps someone with a bit more experience may immediately recognize my problem.

I am trying to estimate the parameters (c0, c1, c2, c3) of a modified circle equation, y = sqrt(a^2 - x^2)*(c0 + c1*(xa) + c2*(xa^2) + c3*(xa^3)) to model the shape of birds' eggs. I am pretty sure that nls is the best way to estimate these parameters.

For example, I have the outline of an egg (well, half), taken from a photograph, in the attached file.

I know, by eye-fitting the parameters, approximately the "correct" ones (roughly .68, .18, .01, .01 in the following example), but even closely bounding these known values produces less-than usable values (it always guesses the parameters as the lowest possible, even when that is a bad fit).
____________________________________________________________________________________________
And the code (its kind of messy, sorry).

work<-read.table("BBOE_3_1_egg1_2009_6_09_a_half.txt")
colnames(work) <- c("x", "y")
a<-.5*(max(work$x)-min(work$x)) #find length of egg
xb<-work$x-a #center at 0
xb<-(xb/a) #scale x values of egg to [-1, 1]

yb<-(work$y/a) #scale y values to the same scale (i guess this assumes pixel squares
#look this up for confirmation)

###analysis, outputting parameter estimates at each iteration
worka<-nls(yb ~ sqrt(xb^2+a^2)*(g + d*(xb/a) + e*((xb/a)^2) + f*((xb/a)^3)),
 start=list(g=.7,d=.2,e=0.01,f=0.01), algorithm = "port",
 lower=list(g=.65, d=.1, e=0, f=0), upper=list(g=.75, d=.3, e=.2, f=.2),
 control = list(maxiter = 50), trace = TRUE)

_____________________________________________________________________________________________________________

For what it is worth: I can generate an egg using the aforementioned formula, and nls will estimate the parameters correctly nomatter what I set the intial values or bounds as (but never converge, which is expected given the perfect fit). This makes me suspect the problem is something about the variance (though there is not a huge amount in the real data- the outline is pretty good).

Anyone have any ideas? Or perhaps any other ideas on a way to attack this problem not using nls?

Thanks,
Eric

It looks like signs are switched in the first term of the nls equation. xb^2+a^2 should be a^2-xb^2.

Also, once you have normalized the x and y values, shouldn’t a=1? When I change the equation to reflect this, it looks like it fits it correctly:

 start=list(g=.7,d=.2,e=0.1,f=0.1),  algorithm = "port",
 lower=list(g=.65, d=.1, e=0, f=0), upper=list(g=.75, d=.3, e=.2, f=.2),

I'm trying to look at multi-collinearity for mixed linear models. I used lmer for the model. The vif function from "car" package deal with only an lm or glm object. I am looking for an equivalent function of VIF which works with lmer objects.

I searched several R-help lists and stackoverflow, but haven't found anything that could solve the problem.

Does anyone have any ideas?

I would really appreciate!

Jane

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: vif function for lmer object
messages.body_plain:
There was a package called AED written by Zuur et al and shared as part of their 2009 book "Mixed effects models and extensions in ecology with R" (blue-purple one with penguins on the cover, also available from our library as an e-book). The package included a function called 'corvif' that helps identify variables with high inflation factors for GLMMs. The authors no longer update AED for new versions of R, but you can download the code at their website  http://www.highstat.com/book2.htm.

I seem to recall I had to make a few modifications to make it run properly, but it worked like a charm after the tweeks. Plus the book gives you guidance on how to properly use the function.

Hope that helps!
Anna
